items.title: Oti-sud/ 4e session ordinaire de la commune 2 : Les travaux consacrés en priorité à l’élaboration du budget primitif exercice 2027
items.description: Mango, 22 oct. (ATOP) – La commune Oti-Sud 2 a tenu du 14 au 19 octobre, la première partie de sa 4 e session à Takpamba, à 54 Km au sud-ouest de Mango. Les travaux ont tourné autour de l’élaboration du budget primitif exercice 2027 suivant les nouvelles orientations du ministère en charge de la Décentralisation, notamment l’étude et l’adoption de la situation financière au 30 septembre. D’autres sujets notamment la signature des contrats avec des agents de la mairie, des échanges sur des stratégies à mettre en branle pour mobiliser davantage des ressources financières, des propositions pour combler l’insuffisance des agents collecteurs dans cantons, les questions en lien avec l’assainissement, la santé, l’environnement, l’éducation dans les cantons ont été aussi abordés. Oti-sud/ 4e session ordinaire de la commune 2 Cette session se tient conformément à l’article 93 de la loi sur la Décentralisation et les libertés locales. Elle a regroupé des élus locaux, des responsables des services déconcentrés de l’Etat, des garants des us et coutumes, des Forces de Défense et de Sécurité (FDS), des responsables des associations et d’ONG et des partenaires de la commune. La session a permis d’amener des acteurs impliqués dans l’élaboration de ce budget à faire des propositions qui tiennent compte des réalités de cette communes et des directives du ministère en charge de la décentralisation. Il s’agissait d’analyser et adopter la situation financière de la commune à la fin du mois de septembre ; relever les insuffisances dans la mobilisation des recettes, recueillir des propositions pour mieux renflouer les caisses de la commune. La présentation de la situation financière révèle que les recettes des mois de juillet à septembre se chiffrent à 40.652.647FCFA, ceci, du au fait que cette commune a bénéficié au cours de cette période, du Fonds d’appui aux collectivités territoriale qui s’élevé à plus de 37 millions de FCFA. Quant aux dépenses sur cette même période, elles s’enlèvent à 3.727.395 FCFA. Le solde est excédentaire de 27.426.277FCFA. Pour le problème lié à la collecte des taxes, il est ressorti que dans cette commune, des jeunes ne veulent pas exercer le métier de collecteurs dans les cantons les quatre cantons ce qui fait chuter la mobilisation des ressources. Le préfet de l’Oti-Sud, Sambiani Fékimani Félix a félicité les élus locaux pour leur engagement à œuvrer pour le développement de cette commune. Il les a exhortés à toujours travailler en toute responsabilité et a suivre à la lettre les consignes du ministere en charge de la Décentralisaton dans l’élaboration du budget primitif qui constitue la boussole pour la commune dans la gestion éfficace des ressources disponibles. Le préfet a suggéré à la commune de mettre sur pied un comité pour gérer les questions liées à l’assainissement dans les cantons afin de se prémunir contre des maladies liées à l’insalubrité en cette période de fortes pluies. Il a réitéré sa disponibilité à accompagner cette commune dans l’atteinte de ses objectifs Le maire de la commune Oti-Sud 2, Mme Koulalo Tieba Dzigbondi a exhorté ses paires et les participants à participer activement aux travaux et à faire des propositions pertinentes pour booster le développement endogène. Mme Koulalo a insisté qu’il ait un dialogue permanent entre les populations et la mairie ajoutant que le développement de la commune incombe à tout le monde et nécessite la participation de tous. Elle a fait remarquer que sa commune est engagée à investir dans les secteurs de la santé, de l’éducation, des infrstructures socio de base, de l’assainissement et autres et nécessite la participation de tous . Elle a remercié le prefet pour ses conseils et appuis pour le dévéloppement de la commune. Les travaux ont été suspendu, en attendant le mois de décembre pour la poursuite des travaux en vue de l’adoption du budget prévisionnel. ATOP/TT/KYA

items.title: NDC bars Communicator from media appearances over remarks on alleged rape by Obuasi SHTS head
items.description: The National Democratic Congress (NDC) has barred its Amasaman Communications Officer, Daniel Nortey, from all media appearances and public engagements on behalf of the party following controversial remarks he made while commenting on the alleged rape of female students by the interdicted headmaster of the Obuasi Senior High Technical School, Zakaria Abdulai, who’s also the NDC’s Juaben Constituency Secretary. The suspension, announced by the party’s Communication Directorate in a statement on Thursday, October 22, takes immediate effect and will remain in place until further notice. This comes after Mr Nortey sparked public outrage during a panel discussion on Accra-based ATV when he questioned the seriousness of rape allegations and made remarks suggesting that the act was not unusual. “He’s a rapist, and so what? Haven’t you done that before? Is today the first time someone is raping someone?” he said during the discussion. He also turned to another panellist and asked whether the person had raped someone before. The comments drew widespread criticism, prompting Mr Nortey to issue an apology on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, in a video shared by Accra-based Okay FM on Facebook. In the apology, he said the remarks were made during a heated discussion and did not reflect his position on rape. “During the interview, we were having heated discussions, and so, in the heat of the moment, I ended up making such remarks, which I have regretted. So I am asking for forgiveness from Ghanaians and anyone who has been affected by my comments,” he said. Mr Nortey appealed to women, Ghanaians and party executives to forgive him, insisting that he did not support rape and would take the matter seriously if any of his female relatives became victims. “I’m appealing to women and Ghanaians to forgive me. I have sisters and daughters as well, and there is no way I will support rape issues. In fact, if any of my female relatives becomes a victim, I will not take the issue lightly,” he stated. He also expressed respect for women, citing his relationship with his mother, and appealed to the party’s constituency and national executives for forgiveness. “I adore and respect my mother very much, and in the same vein, I accord the same respect to every woman. My constituency, NDC and national executives should forgive me. My intentions were not to cause harm, but it has happened, and I apologise,” he added. In its statement announcing the suspension, the NDC Communication Directorate said it viewed Mr Nortey’s remarks with “serious concern and distaste”. The party reiterated its zero-tolerance stance on sexual abuse and all forms of sexual exploitation, particularly where the safety, dignity and welfare of children are concerned. It condemned comments that trivialise allegations of sexual abuse or undermine the seriousness with which such cases must be treated. Although the Directorate acknowledged Mr Nortey’s unreserved apology, it stressed that public commentary on allegations of sexual abuse must be guided by responsibility, sensitivity and respect for due process. “Such matters must not be treated lightly or reduced to partisan debate,” the statement said. The party reaffirmed its commitment to protecting women and children, promoting accountability and ensuring that allegations of sexual abuse are handled with the seriousness they deserve and in accordance with the law. The controversy comes amid public attention surrounding allegations of sexual abuse against Mr Abdulai, following a JoyNews investigation by Manasseh Azure Awuni titled Inside the Dreaded Headmaster’s Bungalow .

items.title: Ghana’s hospitals are adopting AI, but the machines were never trained on Ghanaian patients
items.description: An algorithm that reads chest X-rays learns by looking at tens of thousands of them. It learns what a normal lung looks like, what tuberculosis looks like, what a tumour looks like, by being shown examples until the pattern sticks. The question nobody asks at the point of purchase is whose lungs it was shown. If the answer is Boston and Berlin and Seoul, and the lung now in front of it belongs to a farmer in Bolgatanga, the machine is working from a reference population that does not include him. It will still return an answer. It will return it with the same confident interface and the same clean percentage it would give a patient in Massachusetts. It just has a higher chance of being wrong, and nothing on the screen will tell the clinician which case this is. That gap is what I spent months reporting for Biased by Design: The Human Cost , an investigative documentary on the deployment of artificial intelligence in Ghana’s health system, supported by a UK Government media capacity building programme. This is not a future problem The temptation is to file AI in healthcare under things Ghana will have to think about eventually. That is already out of date. AI-assisted tools are in Ghanaian facilities now. Computer-aided detection has been used in tuberculosis screening. Smartphone-based ultrasound support is in the hands of midwives in places where there is no sonographer within an hour’s drive. Ghanaian companies are building diagnostic models domestically, among them MinoHealth, founded by Darlington Akogo, who also chairs the UN ITU and WHO focus group work on artificial intelligence for radiology. Some of this is unambiguously good, and the reporting did not pretend otherwise. A midwife with a tool that flags an abnormal presentation is better equipped than a midwife with nothing. In a country with the specialist shortages Ghana has, that is not a small thing. But adoption has run ahead of governance. The people absorbing the risk are the people with the least ability to see it. What the reporting showed I went into this expecting a story about technology. What I came out with was a story about absent rules. The reporting took me to the people on every side of the tool. Darlington Akogo of MinoHealth, building diagnostic models in Accra. Esi Appiah Hagan, a radiographer and global health strategist. Dr Yussif Adams, Senior Lecturer and Head of Biomedical Sciences at the University for Development Studies. Dr Achumboro Aghana Paul, founder of MorphoAI at UDS. Mary Otopah, a Senior Midwifery Officer using AI-assisted ultrasound on real patients in a real facility. Laboratory scientists and innovators working on the problem from inside Ghanaian institutions. What connected them was not disagreement about whether the technology works. It was that not one of them could point me to a Ghanaian rule governing how it enters a hospital, who checks it, or what happens when it is wrong. The clinician at the bedside is left carrying a judgement that should have been made long before the tool reached her, by a regulator, a procurement officer, or a validation study that was never run. The three questions nobody is answering Who approved it? When a hospital in Ghana installs an AI tool that influences a diagnosis, which body signed off on it? Medical devices fall under a regulatory regime. Software that makes a clinical recommendation sits in a grey zone that most countries, Ghana included, are still writing rules for. If no regulator has validated a tool’s performance on a Ghanaian population, the hospital buying it is relying entirely on the vendor’s own claims. Who is accountable when it is wrong? A radiologist who misses a lesion is answerable to a professional body. An algorithm is not. The liability question runs through the vendor, the hospital, the clinician who accepted or overrode the output, and the procurement officer who signed the contract. In Ghana, that chain has not been tested, and nobody wants to be the first case that tests it. Whose data trains the next version? Many of these systems improve by learning from the cases they process. If Ghanaian patient data is being used to refine a model owned elsewhere, Ghanaians are supplying the raw material for a product they will later pay to license. That is not a hypothetical arrangement. It is the standard commercial model, and it is operating in a country whose Data Protection Commission only began enforcement spot checks this month. The African-led answer The more hopeful finding was that the correction is already being attempted from inside the continent. There are Ghanaian researchers and founders building models on local data, in local institutions, with local populations in the reference set. That work is real and it deserves support. But it is a handful of people against a global pipeline with enormous capital behind it. Without procurement rules that ask what a tool was trained on, without a regulator that can validate performance locally, and without data governance that tells Ghanaians what happens to their scans, the default keeps winning. The default is a system that was never trained on us, making decisions about us, with nobody required to say so out loud. Ghana’s answer cannot be to refuse the technology. The shortages are too severe and the potential is too real. The answer is to insist on the question that no procurement form currently asks. Whose data taught this machine, and does it include mine? Dr. Emmanuel Raphael Samani is a medical laboratory scientist and a broadcast journalist with JoyNews. His documentary Biased by Design: The Human Cost examines the deployment of artificial intelligence in Ghana’s health system.

items.title: The Limits of the Cinematic Universe
items.description: Sign up for Video Village , a new weekly newsletter in which David Sims unearths cinematic gems and brings readers into his movie obsession. When James Gunn was named a co-head of DC Studios in 2022, along with his producing partner Peter Safran, he was essentially being tasked with building a plane in midair. His remit from Warner Bros. (which owns DC Comics and its entertainment rights) was to clear away the dregs of its most recent efforts to create a cinematic superhero universe, quickly reboot things with a slate of new comic-book movies, and direct the first big entry himself, which turned out to be 2025’s Superman . The studio had spent years trying to play catch-up with Disney’s hugely successful Marvel movies, pumping out films either directed by Zack Snyder or made to suit his darker tone, and although some had hit, the overall project never seemed to find cultural ubiquity. So with Gunn (who made the hit Guardians of the Galaxy trilogy for Marvel) aboard, DC is trying again. But it’s happening as the state of genre cinema seems to be shifting away from the “cinematic universe” approach. Yes, Marvel’s still making movies, at a slightly more relaxed pace, but the many other imitators have wound down (think of Sony’s flimsy villain-focused attempts at a wider Spider-Man world, Fox’s now-collapsed X-Men universe, or failed efforts such as Universal’s “Dark Universe”). Audiences have grown savvy to the treadmill these series put them on, with each ending teasing future editions rather than providing satisfying conclusions, characters never getting happy endings, and fun cameos by past and future members of the universe substituting for actually interesting writing. Gunn and Safran, to their credit, seem somewhat self-aware about the problems that can sprout from the cinematic universe. In addition to narrative stagnation, these movies have a sort of necessary homogeneity. Part of what makes the Marvel brand “work” is that super-producer and honcho Kevin Feige has overarching creative control, so there’s a consistent tone—but also a bit of sameness to the visuals, the action, even the humor. Every movie starts filming with reshoots built in and scripts sometimes unfinished, more like the creation of a television show. So Gunn said things at DC would work differently: Movies could be green-lighted only with finished scripts , directors could put their imprimatur on whatever project they were in charge of, and entries in a given series could vary wildly in terms of genre and content. That’s why Clayface is such an interesting test case for the entire DC endeavor. The leadoff film in this universe, Gunn’s Superman , was a genuine delight, but it was very much a comic-book movie, aimed at the widest audience possible with a pretty sunny, bouncy PG-13 tone. The second effort was this summer’s Supergirl , inarguably a misfire from Craig Gillespie ( I, Tonya ) that aimed for darkly cynical but felt anonymous. Clayface is at least offering the hope of something fresh. It’s a gory, R-rated horror movie about a Batman villain who seems connected to the wider DC universe in only the slimmest of ways. The film is about an up-and-coming actor named Matt Hagen (played by Tom Rhys Harries) whose face is disfigured after a brutal attack from a gangster. He seeks experimental nanotechnology treatment to rebuild it and soon finds himself with weird “powers”—sometimes he can shape-shift into another person entirely; other times his features look like they’re melting off his skull. Clayface is essentially a visual-effects-driven body-horror movie with some impressive, gory flourishes; its only real connection to the DC Universe is that it’s set in Gotham City. I enjoyed it, while finding it rather silly, but was a little baffled by its existence in the first place. That’s because Clayface is, indeed, a member of Batman’s rogues’ gallery in comic books, a big gooey monster that the Caped Crusader occasionally does battle with. But Gunn’s new version of this world has yet to establish who will play Batman (the recent Robert Pattinson movie is not included in it), and there’s no immediate plan to do so. In a way, that’s wise (Hollywood is saturated with Batmen already), but Clayface is a minor-key work that struggles to justify itself. What worries me the most about the ongoing DC plan is that, ultimately, there may be no way to create a cinematic universe that doesn’t require a level of Marvel-like rigor. Gunn is green-lighting interesting things, and he’s had some decent success on the TV side too: The relatively gripping Lanterns is getting good ratings on HBO Max; the hilarious-sounding mockumentary The People vs. Gorilla Grodd is coming in 2027. But he’s moving at a much slower pace, which makes an oddity such as Clayface feel inessential—yes, it’s a tiny piece of a bigger landscape, but when we see only one or two works a year, that landscape is filling in too slowly for us to get invested. Marvel’s approach of total saturation was overwhelming for many, but there may be no other way to make the grander project feel worthwhile. An Essay I Enjoyed Illustration by Marine Buffard 50 Unforgettable Love Stories By The Atlantic Culture Desk Centuries before bookstores had shelves labeled ROMANCE and fictional hockey players locked eyes across the ice, the love story, with all of its attendant joys and sorrows, was an organizing principle of life—and of literature. The sentiment that another person might “complete” us enchanted both Plato and Jerry Maguire, and the search for that someone, along with the desire to understand why it can hurt so bad, has animated fiction from the beginning. The list below is an effort to name those love stories: novels, of course, but also poetry, plays, and short stories—that we consider to be the most enduring. We asked a jury of scholars, librarians, critics, and authors across genres, as well as many colleagues, to name their favorite titles that were originally written in English. We thought of our own personal touchstones, deliberated over the choices, and emerged with a group of standouts: 50 titles you won’t soon forget. Read the full article. Coming Attractions Last week I wrote about the industry turmoil going on at Warner Bros. as it merged with Paramount under the Skydance umbrella, with the storied executives Michael De Luca and Pam Abdy suddenly finding themselves out of a job after a string of misses in 2026. Well, their next opportunity might be arriving very quickly, because Netflix is the next movie studio to see turnover up top. First, “chief content officer” Bela Bajaria was axed on October 15; then her subordinate Dan Lin (who ran its film division) was informed he was out a day later. Lin had been hired in 2024 to rein in spending; a somewhat confusing New York Times profile of him this year said the studio was “done coddling Hollywood,” an oddly aggressive bit of press for a company that’s already struggling to attract top talent because of its hostility to cinema releases. Now Netflix is seemingly looking to pivot back to prestige, abandoning the belt-tightening that went on under Lin. De Luca and Abdy, who are reportedly in talks to take over, would provide an instant shot of it, given their existing relationships with big auteurs including Ryan Coogler and Paul Thomas Anderson, and they are reportedly discussing guaranteed theatrical releases, something Netflix has only just begun to tiptoe toward. It’s already happening with movies such as Greta Gerwig’s Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew , David Fincher’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth , and now the KPop Demon Hunters sequel. But could Netflix actually abandon one of its biggest tenets in search of Hollywood luster? To fill the gap being left by Warner Bros. and the merger, maybe. What Else I’m Watching The wide release most worth checking out in theaters this week is Wildwood , the epic stop-motion animated adventure directed by Travis Knight (the company’s CEO, who also directed Kubo and the Two Strings ). Wildwood , based on the first entry in Colin Meloy’s Wildwood Chronicles novels, has been in development for 15 years and in production for five, and really feels like a true labor of love. That can be said about every movie from Laika, a stop-motion studio based out of Oregon that made its name with Coraline . The films are all huge undertakings made more for artistic enjoyment than for profit, but Wildwood is especially ambitious, featuring PG-13 action and a two-plus-hour running time. Take your older kids to see and enjoy—it’s a fun modern fantasy as well as an affectionate portrait of Portland, where Knight grew up. There’s also Wicker , a sweet folk comedy that I heartily enjoyed, starring Olivia Colman as a reclusive fisherwoman who contracts a local weaver (Peter Dinklage) to make her a husband out of wicker. And indeed he does, creating a creature (Alexander Skarsgard) that looks like a handsome scarecrow and rustles romantically with every step. It has the potential to be a horror movie, but it’s actually a wry satire of patriarchal relations in medieval times (and how, in some ways, things have never changed). Colman is, as always, a true comic delight.

items.title: Ghanaian clinic stored patient records on an unassessed system before regulator intervened
items.description: Ghana’s Data Protection Commission has moved from persuasion to enforcement. What it found in one clinic raises harder questions about the national systems now holding the country’s medical records. I spend part of my week in a laboratory and part of it behind a news desk. On the laboratory side, I sign out results. A full blood count. A fasting glucose. A hepatitis B surface antigen that will change how a patient is treated for the rest of their life. The moment I release that result, it stops being a piece of paper. It becomes a row in a database. It travels. It is stored somewhere, by someone, under terms I have never been shown. In nine years of laboratory practice, I have rarely seen a patient told where that information goes, who can see it, or what they are entitled to ask about it. Whether a signature on a consent form was legally required at each of those moments is a genuine question, and the answer is often no. Act 843 recognises several lawful bases for processing beyond consent. But lawful processing is not the same as invisible processing. The Act also requires that patients be given specified information when their data is collected, that the processing be secure, and that patients be able to see and correct what is held about them. That is the test. Not whether anyone signed a form, but whether any of it is being done lawfully, transparently and safely. On 12 October, the Data Protection Commission went to find out. What the inspectors found The Commission’s team visited a clinic. According to Graphic Online’s account of the exercise, published on 13 October, the clinic had not appointed a Data Protection Supervisor. It had unpaid fees going back to at least January 2025. Its organisational and technical measures to protect personal information were inadequate. And it had never carried out a privacy impact assessment of the electronic system in which it stores its patients’ records. The clinic was directed to give a statement to the police. Two hospitals were also visited. Both were registered with the Commission, but their data protection certificates had expired. That is a different finding from never having registered at all, and it carries a different enforcement route. A microfinance company was separately referred to CID headquarters over a lapsed registration and an incomplete compliance report. The Commission’s Executive Director, Dr Arnold Kavaarpuo, has said it can no longer rely on education and persuasion alone, fourteen years after the Act was passed. Its Director of Regulatory and Compliance, Mr Quintin Akrobotu, says the aim is compliance rather than punishment. The Commission recorded 2,575 data controller registrations in 2026, though a registration is a starting point rather than proof that an organisation is compliant. Inspections will continue into 2027 and extend to religious institutions and the media. One inspection cannot tell you how widespread the problem is. It can tell you what nobody was checking for. Why a clinic is a data controller Section 27 of the Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843) requires a data controller intending to process personal data to register with the Commission before doing so. Section 50 provides for renewal every two years. Section 56 makes processing personal data without the required registration punishable on summary conviction by a fine of up to 250 penalty units, imprisonment of up to two years, or both. A data controller is defined by responsibility, not by signage. Any organisation that determines the purposes for which and the manner in which personal data is processed falls within the Act. In practice that captures most hospitals, laboratories, pharmacies, CHPS compounds and private clinics, because each of them decides what to collect about a patient and what to do with it. One such organisation has now been found without a supervisor, without a privacy assessment and without adequate safeguards on a system holding patient records. The reasonable question is not whether that clinic is typical. It is whether anyone knows. The year Ghana’s health records went dark That question lands in the middle of the most disruptive year Ghana’s health information systems have had. The Lightwave Health Information Management System, LHIMS, was introduced in Ghana in 2017, with implementation documented in the Central Region, and was subsequently expanded under a national programme. In 2019 the government signed a contract worth US$100 million to connect 950 health facilities. The Minister of Health, Kwabena Mintah Akandoh, told a briefing on 29 October 2025 that the contract was meant to expire in 2022, was extended twice to the end of 2024, and that at expiry only 450 facilities had been connected. He said about US$77 million had been paid, more than 70 per cent of the contract value, and that the contract never received parliamentary approval. He said the vendor had been switching the system off at will after the ministry required it to hand over data and grant administrative access, and that the system had been completely down for about two weeks. His words were that if that is not blackmailing, he does not know what it is. Those are the Minister’s allegations, not the findings of an independent audit, and the vendor rejects them. Lightwave has disputed the performance calculation, arguing that facilities carried different contractual costs and that its completed deployments represented roughly 72 per cent of the contract’s value. It has also disputed the allegations concerning hosting, access and hardware. Former Health Minister Dr Bernard Okoe-Boye challenged the handling of the termination on JoyNews the same day, arguing the contract should have been wound down in an orderly way, and citing the delivery figure against a different total of 500 units rather than 950 facilities. What is not in dispute is that records became unreachable. MyJoyOnline reported that patient records going back to 2020 had become inaccessible during the disruption. On 29 October 2025 the Ghana Health Service directed all public and mission facilities to adopt the Ghana Health Information Management System, GHIMS, a state-owned platform, as the sole authorised system for patient registration, clinical documentation, insurance verification, billing and NHIA claims. The Minister announced a four-week phased rollout, beginning with teaching and regional hospitals and working down through district hospitals, polyclinics, health centres and CHPS compounds. The unanswered question is what happened to the records Here is what the public record does not establish. A patient walks into a district hospital in 2022. They give their name, their age, their symptoms, their HIV status, their pregnancy history. That information is entered into a system operated under a commercial contract the patient has never seen. Three years later, the government and the vendor are in dispute. Access to records held in that system is disrupted. The government announces a replacement platform. What remains unclear is the extent to which those historical records have been preserved, made accessible, and transferred to the new system. The Ministry and the vendor disagreed publicly about access to the existing data. Nobody has published an account of what happened to it. At no point in that chain is it clear what patients were told about how their records would be stored, who would have access to them, or what would happen to their information when the system changed. The questions the Commission put to one clinic on 12 October apply with far greater force to the national systems: How many of Ghana’s teaching, regional and district hospitals are registered with the Commission, and how many hold current certificates? Was a privacy impact assessment carried out before GHIMS was deployed, or before patient records were moved onto it? Who is the designated data protection supervisor for the Ghana Health Service, and for the Ministry of Health? What legal basis applies to each stage of processing, and what were patients told at the point of collection? Section 32 of Act 843 gives patients the right to access and correct their records. Can a Ghanaian patient exercise that right today and get a response? The last one is not academic. A right that nobody can exercise in practice is not a right, it is decoration. Sovereignty is the easy half The government has framed the move to GHIMS as a sovereignty win, and there is something in that. A state-controlled platform can strengthen public oversight of health information systems, and a vendor should not be able to turn the lights off during a contract dispute. But the LHIMS episode shows why the distinction matters. Lightwave has said the Ministry of Health owned the patient data while the company owned the software intellectual property. The Ministry disputed aspects of that account, including access and hosting. Ownership of the data, ownership of the software, control of the infrastructure, and the practical ability to access and recover patient records are four separate questions. A system can be locally controlled and still fail its patients if governance, security and continuity arrangements are inadequate. There is still time. GHIMS is new, and it is an opportunity to build privacy protections into the registration workflow, to publish a register of health sector data controllers, and to assess the privacy risks attached to the new system and to any movement of patient records onto it. Act 843 already establishes the core obligations around lawful processing, transparency, data security and the protection of data subject rights. The Commission’s own guidance provides a framework for assessing and mitigating privacy risk. Ghana has built the pipes. The Data Protection Commission has started enforcing the law. The two conversations have not yet met. They should meet before the next outage, not after.

items.title: China bets on manufactured water, and wants to sell it to the world
items.description: China is emerging as a major supplier of water technology to parched countries across Asia, the Middle East and Africa, as shrinking natural supplies at home push Beijing to invest heavily in manufactured freshwater, industry experts say. Chinese firms are selling desalination membranes, filtration equipment and engineering services to Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, often through the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), which connects Chinese capital and infrastructure projects to developing markets. Even Gulf states, long desalination pioneers, are turning to Chinese manufacturers to produce equipment at scale. China exported more than $2 billion of water filtering and purifying machinery in 2025, up 25 per cent from $1.6bn in 2020, according to UN Comtrade . Vontron Technology said it shipped more than 30,000 seawater desalination membranes to BRI countries last year, enough for more than 300,000 tons of daily capacity. In January, PowerChina said it was building a water supply project in Tanzania to serve more than 450,000 people. At home, Beijing has made water security a strategic priority. Spending on water conservancy has grown faster than military spending since 2015, according to China Water Risk (CWR), a Hong Kong-based think tank. It now exceeds 1.2 trillion yuan ($170bn) a year, which CWR says rivals China’s central military budget. A crisis at home The push is rooted in domestic risk. In August, a massive collapse of ice and rock near the border between Nepal and Tibet showed how volatile natural water sources are becoming. Tibet’s “water towers” feed headwaters for nearly 2bn people across South, Southeast and East Asia, and climate change is eroding them. Meanwhile, severe over-extraction in northern China has depleted groundwater and left key farming regions with systemic deficits. “We could see peak water by 2050 across 10 major river systems that provide water to one in two Asians as glacier melt peaks and river flows decline,” CWR said. Peak water is the tipping point where flows from natural water sources reach a maximum and thereafter enter continual decline. “This will put almost half the GDP of 16 countries at risk, including China, CWR said. Benjamin Horton, dean of the School of Energy and Environment at City University of Hong Kong, said China’s ability to develop water technology at scale could cut costs for other water-stressed countries. He said Beijing could become Asia’s leading provider of practical water security solutions. “Through the Belt and Road Initiative, there is likely to be continued demand for hydropower, desalination, flood forecasting, irrigation, wastewater treatment, and climate-resilient infrastructure,” he said. Water as national security In July, China rolled out new regulations under its Five-Year Plan that treat water as a pillar of national security and economic self-reliance, not just an environmental issue. Surface water supplies about 80pc of China’s freshwater, while recycled water, desalinated seawater and harvested rainwater provide just 3pc to 4pc. Authorities have pledged to raise that share. The South-North Water Transfer Project moves billions of cubic meters from the Yangtze to the dry north, but it is constrained by energy costs and shrinking surpluses in the warming Yangtze basin. Saleh Al Khabti, China president of Saudi developer Acwa, said costs are rising and quality is deteriorating in some areas. China operated 167 seawater desalination projects at the end of 2025, with total capacity of 3,076,805 tonnes a day, up 221,283 tonnes from 2024, according to the Ministry of Natural Resources. State media put the average production cost at 4 to 8 yuan per cubic meter. Industry reports expect the market to grow from $1.84bn in 2024 to $4.66bn in 2033, or about 11pc a year. Hurdles remain, including the scale of investment and the central planning needed for multi-city conveyance grids, while public attitudes also pose a challenge. Khabti said many Chinese still view drinking desalinated water as taboo, though local governments are keen to build capacity. Foreign players buying in Khabti said more than 90pc of the renewable equipment Acwa procures comes from Chinese manufacturers, and the company buys about 70pc of its global water equipment from Chinese suppliers. Acwa has pledged to invest up to $30bn in China by 2030, working with firms including PowerChina and China Energy Engineering Corporation. It plans to spend at least $15bn a year on Chinese equipment over the next three years across renewables, green hydrogen and desalination. Khabti expects Chinese membrane makers to catch up fast. “It took us 15 years to reach where we are today with our partners,” he said. He thinks Chinese original equipment manufacturers could match that level in two to three years, and he expects desalination to follow wind and solar as “a big area of exports.” “We’re very bullish about China,” he said. “Once it’s there, China will be the leader.”

items.title: Ghana needs a dedicated hospitality school to improve standards – Ridge Royal Hotel MD
items.description: The Managing Director of Ridge Royal Hotel in Cape Coast in the Central Region, Sheila Adjetey-Anum, has called for the establishment of a dedicated hospitality school in the country to train and equip hospitality workers with practical skills to improve service delivery. She said existing university programmes often emphasise classroom learning at the expense of the hands-on training needed to meet international hospitality standards. Speaking in an interview with Myjoyonline on the sidelines of the ongoing iNTTA Expo at Ridge Royal Hotel on Thursday, October 22, she said a specialised institution would complement existing university programmes by providing practical industry experience. “Yes, universities like UCC and all that, they do actually offer tourism. But it’s not just theory we’re looking for. We’re looking for hands-on, practical training,” she said. She explained that a dedicated hospitality school would give students first-hand experience in hospitality operations and prepare them for the demands of the job market. “Hotel school isn’t taking away from the universities; but there’s so much difference between having a hotel school where you actually get training, not just theory, but also practice,” she added. Ms Adjetey-Anum said such an institution would help workers understand professional service standards and enable Ghana’s hospitality industry to compete more effectively internationally. “How do we get to meet their expectations when we don’t have institutions to support us in terms of training to get us where we need to get to?” she asked. The call comes as industry stakeholders gather for the iNTTA Expo in Cape Coast, which is bringing together tourism and hospitality players, businesses and investors to explore opportunities for investment and growth in the sector. The expo’s second day, held under the theme “From Vision to Transactions”, is focusing on investment opportunities across tourism, hospitality, energy, digital infrastructure, agribusiness and health tourism.

items.title: Sudan hunger crisis deepens as aid cuts collide with crop failure in Darfur
items.description: Cuts to food aid and a near-total crop failure are leaving displaced families and vulnerable communities struggling to find food as prices soar and malnutrition worsens. Cuts to World Food Programme (WFP) assistance threaten displaced families across Sudan, while a near-total crop failure in East Darfur has left households short of food and income. Residents of Sheairia report soaring prices, worsening malnutrition, and shortages of medicines and therapeutic food for children. In a statement to reporters following an eight-day visit to Sudan last month, the WFP’s acting executive director, Carl Skau, says the agency has the capacity to reach millions of people caught between war, displacement and worsening drought – but is running out of money. The General Coordination for Displaced People and Refugees now warns that reduced food assistance could force families to skip meals and sell their remaining possessions to survive. Adam Rijal, the coordination body’s spokesperson, told Radio Dabanga that funding shortages and cuts to WFP assistance could deprive displaced families of essential meals and force them to adopt increasingly desperate coping strategies, including withdrawing children from school, selling their remaining possessions, and reducing the number and size of meals. Children, women, older people, and people with disabilities face particular risks of malnutrition and disease, he said, calling on donors and international institutions to close the funding gap and ensure food assistance reaches those most in need. Distribution of seeds to small farmers in the Um Shujaira area of ​​Sha’iriya locality, East Darfur – July 2026 (Photo: Supplied) Failed harvests deepen food insecurity The warning comes as residents of Sheairia locality in East Darfur report a near-total failure of the agricultural season, sharply higher food prices, and shortages of medicines for people and livestock. Resident Babiker Ishaq told Radio Dabanga that farmers had harvested almost nothing of their main crops, including groundnuts, millet, sorghum, and okra. The losses have deprived households of a crucial source of food and income, leaving some unable to find enough to eat amid the absence of humanitarian assistance. A sack of millet costs about SDG 350,000 when paid for through bank transfers, while a sack of sorghum costs a similar amount, Ishaq said. A pound of onions costs around SDG 4,500, a bottle of cooking oil between SDG 13,000 and SDG 14,000, and a pound of sugar about SDG 4,000 when paid for through bank transfers. He said deductions on transfers through the Bankak app, which he estimated at 40% in some cases and 50% in others, further reduce the money available to families for essential purchases. Malnutrition and medicine shortages The food crisis is also affecting children and pregnant women. Ishaq said pregnant women were unable to obtain adequate diets and children were suffering from malnutrition, while supplies of therapeutic food were limited. He called for increased supplies to treat malnourished children and urgent deliveries of medicines and medical supplies. Livestock are also at risk because of shortages of veterinary medicines. Ishaq reported illnesses among cattle, horses, and donkeys, adding that about six or seven children had reportedly been bitten by dogs suspected of having rabies. A rabies treatment injection costs about SDG 300,000, he said, putting it beyond the reach of many families. Calls for urgent humanitarian assistance Rijal called on donors and international institutions to maintain food assistance, strengthen nutrition and food security programmes, and prioritise the worst-affected areas. He also urged the authorities to ensure safe, unhindered access for aid deliveries and called for an end to the war and a humanitarian truce to allow relief to reach civilians. Ishaq appealed to humanitarian and health organisations to provide food, medicines, therapeutic nutrition supplies, and veterinary care to protect both residents and the livestock on which many families depend. items.title: Benmoussa présente l’approche marocaine en matière de renforcement de la cohésion sociale
items.description: Le Haut-Commissaire au Plan, Chakib Benmoussa, a présenté, jeudi à Marrakech, l'approche du Maroc en matière de renforcement de la cohésion et des liens sociaux ainsi que de consécration de la solidarité au sein de la société. Intervenant à la conférence inaugurale d’un séminaire international organisé par le Conseil international d’action sociale (ICSW), sous le thème « De l'exclusion à l'appartenance : Promouvoir les pratiques inclusives pour renforcer les liens sociaux et communautaires », M. Benmoussa a mis en lumière les avancées et les réalisations enregistrées par le Maroc dans ce domaine, soulignant que l’édification de l’État social constitue une priorité nationale, donnant lieu à plusieurs réformes et chantiers structurants visant à garantir à chaque citoyen les conditions d’une vie digne, à promouvoir l’égalité des chances et à consolider la cohésion sociale. « Sous l’impulsion de Sa Majesté le Roi Mohammed VI, le Maroc a engagé, au cours des dernières années, une série d’initiatives et de réformes destinées à renforcer les fondements de l’État social et à consolider les mécanismes de solidarité, en veillant à réduire les disparités sociales et territoriales et à favoriser une plus grande inclusion de l’ensemble des catégories de la population » , a-t-il relevé. Il a, dans ce cadre, cité le rôle de la Fondation Mohammed V pour la Solidarité, qui agit en partenariat avec les associations de la société civile pour répondre aux besoins des populations confrontées aux aléas climatiques et aux catastrophes naturelles et aux déficits sociaux dans les quartiers urbains défavorisés. Benmoussa a aussi évoqué l’Initiative Nationale pour le Développement Humain (INDH), qui a largement contribué à faire reculer la pauvreté et l’exclusion et à réduire les disparités entre les régions, ainsi que le chantier de la généralisation de la protection sociale, engagé conformément aux hautes orientations royales, et qui consacre le principe de solidarité nationale et vise à garantir à chaque citoyen un socle de protection intégré et équitable, avec une attention particulière accordée aux personnes les plus vulnérables. Et de relever que ces efforts traduisent une vision globale, qui considère la solidarité et l'inclusion comme des leviers essentiels pour consolider le lien social et réduire les disparités. Mettant l’accent sur les transformations profondes qui affectent la famille, qu'il s'agisse de l'évolution de sa structure, de ses modes de vie ou de ses fonctions, Benmoussa a souligné la place particulière que le Royaume accorde à cette institution, pilier de la société et premier espace de solidarité et de transmission des valeurs. Dans son intervention, il a aussi abordé les défis démographiques, technologiques et climatiques auxquels les pays sont confrontés, relevant que ces mutations accélérées exigent l'adoption d'approches anticipatives, de nature à permettre aux politiques publiques d'accompagner efficacement les transformations en cours. Dans cette perspective, il a fait observer que le Maroc dispose d'un système statistique performant, en mesure d'accompagner les politiques publiques et de mesurer avec exactitude l'impact des politiques sur les citoyens. Benmoussa a, par ailleurs, mis en avant le rôle important que jouent la cohésion sociale et la solidarité dans la lutte contre l'isolement et l'exclusion, notamment dans un contexte marqué par l'augmentation du nombre de personnes âgées, précisant que le renforcement des liens entre les générations apparait comme un enjeu majeur pour bâtir une société inclusive, solidaire et résiliente. Co-organisé par ICSW Europe et ICSW MENA, cet événement international, qui se poursuit jusqu’au 24 octobre, vise à identifier des approches pratiques, innovantes et reproductibles pour renforcer les liens communautaires et réduire la solitude et l'isolement social. Lors de cette rencontre, une attention particulière sera accordée aux défis spécifiques à chaque région et aux pratiques émergentes en Europe et dans la région MENA, avec un accent sur les enseignements transférables et les solutions concrètes. Les travaux de ce séminaire seront sanctionnés par l’adoption de la Déclaration de Marrakech qui définira les contours du phénomène de l'isolement et les pratiques inclusives à même de renforcer les liens sociaux et communautaires, à la lumière de nouvelles mutations socioéconomiques que connaissent les pays membres du CIAS. The post Benmoussa présente l’approche marocaine en matière de renforcement de la cohésion sociale appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Compétitivité du secteur privé: l’État recense les difficultés des entreprises du Pôle nord
items.description: Le ministère de l’Économie, des Finances et du Plan a ouvert, mardi 20 octobre, à Saint-Louis, deux jours de concertation territoriale avec les entreprises stratégiques du Pôle nord. Cette rencontre a pour objectif d’identifier les contraintes qui freinent l’investissement privé et de dégager des solutions concrètes pour renforcer la compétitivité des entreprises locales, stimuler la création d’emplois et contribuer à la mise en œuvre de la « Vision Sénégal 2050 ». Saint-Louis – Donner davantage de place au secteur privé dans la transformation économique du pays. C’est l’ambition des concertations territoriales organisées, les 20 et 21 octobre, à Saint-Louis, par le ministère de l’Économie, des Finances et du Plan, en collaboration avec les autorités administratives. Les échanges réunissent les entreprises stratégiques autour de leurs difficultés, de leurs perspectives de développement et des mesures attendues des pouvoirs publics. Pour Khoudia Lèye Diouf, adjointe au gouverneur de Saint-Louis chargée du développement, cette initiative offre un cadre privilégié d’expression aux acteurs économiques de la région. « C’est l’occasion d’écouter les entreprises intervenant dans la région, pour qu’elles puissent revenir sur les difficultés auxquelles elles sont confrontées, mais également formuler leurs recommandations », a-t-elle expliqué. Les contributions recueillies doivent permettre de mieux orienter les décisions publiques et de conforter les ambitions de la « Vision Sénégal 2050 ». Au-delà du diagnostic, les autorités veulent donner une traduction opérationnelle aux préoccupations exprimées par les chefs d’entreprise. Aziz Fall, coordonnateur à la Direction générale de la Coopération, des financements extérieurs, du développement du secteur privé et des partenariats, insiste sur la nécessité de passer de l’identification des acteurs économiques à la recherche de solutions adaptées à leurs besoins. « On ne va pas résoudre tous les problèmes en deux jours, mais on va montrer qu’il y a une nouvelle dynamique qui s’enclenche », a-t-il souligné. Cette démarche doit, selon lui, permettre de distinguer les difficultés pouvant être résolues rapidement de celles nécessitant des études techniques, des réformes ou des investissements structurants. M. Fall met également l’accent sur les opportunités offertes par le développement du secteur extractif, notamment l’exploitation du gaz. L’enjeu est que les entreprises locales puissent prendre leur place dans les chaînes de valeur générées par cette activité. « Cette dynamique ne laissera aucune chaîne de valeur en rade, y compris le secteur des hydrocarbures », a-t-il assuré, réaffirmant l’engagement de l’État à accompagner le développement du secteur privé sans discrimination sectorielle. Inscrites dans la Stratégie nationale de développement du secteur privé et de promotion de l’investissement 2025-2029, ces concertations ciblent particulièrement les chaînes de valeur du riz, du tourisme et de l’oignon, considérées comme prioritaires dans le Pôle nord. Les travaux doivent déboucher sur une synthèse des contraintes, des recommandations hiérarchisées et un plan d’action destiné à améliorer l’environnement des affaires. Des rencontres entre entreprises et administration sont également prévues, ainsi que des présentations de projets à fort potentiel de création de richesses et d’emplois. La deuxième journée est consacrée aux travaux thématiques, à l’examen des projets d’investissement et aux visites d’entreprises ciblées. Les conclusions attendues doivent alimenter une feuille de route de suivi-évaluation afin d’assurer la continuité des engagements pris. De son côté, le Président-directeur général de Sénégal Agrogreen, Adama Ba, a souligné les principales difficultés auxquelles sont confrontées les entreprises locales. Elles concernent, dit-il, le foncier, la fiscalité et le financement. Jeanne SAGNA (Correspondante)

items.title: Festival des Terres du Nazinon : La culture au service de la paix et du développement
items.description: La deuxième édition du Festival des Terres du Nazinon s’est ouverte le 19 octobre 2026 à Manga, autour du thème « Unité, Culture, Paix et Jeunesse ». Les organisateurs ambitionnent de faire de ce rendez-vous un cadre de cohésion sociale, de promotion du patrimoine culturel et de création d’opportunités économiques pour les populations du Nazinon. Le Festival des Terres du Nazinon entend renforcer sa contribution à la valorisation du patrimoine culturel et au développement local. La promotrice, Denise Koudougou/Oulon, a réaffirmé sa volonté de faire de cette manifestation un rendez-vous fédérateur, ouvert aux communautés et tourné vers la jeunesse. Placée sous le thème « Unité, Culture, Paix et Jeunesse » , cette édition entend promouvoir la diversité culturelle comme un facteur de rapprochement entre les populations. Pour la promotrice, le festival se veut un espace de rencontre entre les générations et les communautés, mais aussi une tribune d’expression pour les artistes, les artisans et les entrepreneurs culturels. « Nous réaffirmons notre volonté de faire de la culture un instrument d’unité, de paix et de développement », a-t-elle déclaré. À travers les prestations artistiques, les expositions et la promotion des produits locaux, les organisateurs souhaitent contribuer à la transmission des traditions, à la valorisation des talents et au renforcement des liens entre les filles et les fils de la région. La première édition du Festival des Terres du Nazinon avait mobilisé plus de 50 000 participants, selon le patron de l’événement, Jacques Sosthène Dingara. Pour cette deuxième édition, la manifestation passe de quatre jours à une semaine d’activités, traduisant la volonté des organisateurs de consolider les acquis et d’accroître son rayonnement. Au-delà de la célébration culturelle, le festival entend contribuer au développement économique du territoire. La promotrice a notamment insisté sur le potentiel touristique de la région du Nazinon, qui dispose, selon elle, de richesses naturelles, historiques et culturelles encore insuffisamment connues et valorisées. Les sites touristiques, les savoir-faire artisanaux et les expressions culturelles constituent, à ses yeux, des leviers susceptibles de renforcer l’attractivité de la région, de créer des opportunités économiques et d’offrir de nouvelles perspectives à la jeunesse. items.title: PM vows to bring back progress to KP, assails PTI's 'callousness' during its tenures
items.description: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday vowed that the federal government, which now runs Khyber Pakhtunkhwa under governor’s rule, would make every effort possible to “bring back” progress to the province. He made the remarks while chairing a meeting of the apex committee in Peshawar, where he arrived earlier in the day on his first visit to the province since the imposition of governor’s rule and the declaration of emergency on Oct 11. The meeting, attended by Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi, reviewed KP’s overall security situation. Federal ministers and newly appointed provincial advisers were also present. Addressing the committee, PM Shehbaz reiterated that emergency and governor’s rule had to be imposed “under extreme compulsion”. “I promise that we will leave no stone unturned in bringing back the happiness and era of progress to this province, and in the practical realisation of the wishes, aspirations, and dreams of this province’s people that have been shattered due to the worst actions of recent years,” he said. The prime minister affirmed that the Centre “will place all possible resources at your feet”. He added that himself, the Advisory Council led by the governor, the president and the CDF “will ensure that this province, once again, not only matches the other provinces in the race for development, but I would be extremely happy if it moves even further ahead”. The prime minister regretted that “terrorists were summoned back here” after peace had been established, “washing down all sacrifices down the drain”. “There can be no greater enmity with the country than not honouring and respecting such sacrifices, not holding them in esteem,” he remarked, highlighting that young soldiers left their homes and families to defend their country. The premier called for an “all-encompassing analysis as to why this happened”, adding that there was “no worse callousness, criminal negligence, and hostility towards the national interest than this”. He said: “All issues of the people were pushed aside — whether it is education, healthcare, or protecting the lives and property of the people — and [having] matters with terrorists instead. I believe that no other example can be found of such hostility against the country, in terms of their attitudes, detachment, and callousness.” PM Shehbaz asserted that 5,000 police vacancies were not filled, Safe City projects were yet to be completed, the capacity of the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) had not been enhanced significantly, and neither were special measures taken regarding police training. He recalled that all provinces had agreed at the time of the 2010 National Finance Commission Award that KP, being the front-line region in combatting terrorism, needed ample resources. “From 2010 to today, more than Rs800 billion in funds have either already been provided or are being provided under this,” he stressed. “However, not only did it resurface, but the weapons needed to counter terrorism, the required capacity, and the trained officers needed were nowhere to be found.” While saying he would not go into the details, the prime minister emphasised that he had assured the provincial governments of ex-chief ministers Ali Amin Gandapur and Sohail Afridi of the Centre’s full support in the fight against terrorism. “But nothing was done regarding this,” he regretted, adding that the government could not remain a “silent spectator” when a “party was stooping to such enmity against the country” and the economy and society were being destroyed. “Therefore, on this occasion we made this one last effort,” the premier said, referring to the province’s interim handover to the federal government under governor’s rule. Highlighting the Centre’s efforts to stabilise the economy over the past two and a half years, PM Shehbaz remarked, “It wouldn’t have been possible [without] unprecedented partnership between political and military hierarchy.” He said the federal government could not remain a silent spectator when “terrorists were roaming around dancing in all areas of KP, and were ruling over some areas in the evening, and collecting extortion” at a time when the stabilisation of Pakistan’s economy was being acknowledged globally. The prime minister recalled the breakdown of the Oct 3 talks between the Centre and reiterated that his government was “compelled to make this decision” of imposing governor’s rule. PM Shehbaz remarked that the province was “shattered with wounds due to the circumstances created in the past several years”. He highlighted the poor law and order situation over the past six years, recalling that security forces and law enforcement agencies had made sacrifices to establish peace in KP. The premier said there was corruption of Rs100bn in the clean drinking water of the Cities Improvement Project and Rs37bn in the “infamous looting” in the case of the Kohistan District Accounts Office . He said that “80,000 people were martyred and the [economy] suffered a loss of several hundred billion dollars. Only then, in 2018, was peace completely restored in this country”. Describing the province as “very beautiful”, the premier expressed his hope that the government “work hard day and night and speedily make it progress towards development and prosperity”. “This is the province that is the first extremely strong wall of the homeland,” he noted. Centre announces Rs160bn uplift funds, other measures PM Shehbaz later also attended a meeting of the Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC) constituted for 12 districts of KP, which face serious security challenges. CDF Munir was also present on the occasion. The council covers Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, Lakki Marwat, Bannu, Bajaur, Mohmand, Khyber, Kurram, Orakzai, North Waziristan, South Waziristan Upper and South Waziristan Lower. It includes 48 elders and prominent personalities from those districts to ensure local representation. Addressing the ARDC, the prime minister announced that the federal government would provide KP with Rs160bn for development projects. Furthermore, to address the wheat shortage in the province, he said the Centre would provide KP “as much wheat as is needed” from the storages of Pakistan Agricultural Storage and Services Corporation (Passco). “However, there should be no hoarding. And whatever price the Centre provides wheat at, the common man should get wheat at that very price,” the premier emphasised. He went on to assure the ARDC that the federal government will provide “whatever assistance” in operations and resources is needed to fight terrorism. He also said directives have been issued to bolster the CTD and complete Safe City projects. PM Shehbaz also asserted that any difficulties in the completion of the federal government’s projects in KP will be resolved, adding that the governor-led administration will address problems in provincial projects. The prime minister appreciated the tribal elders for always supporting Pakistan unequivocally and said the ARDC now had an “immense responsibility”. Noting the remarks of ARDC Chairman Shaukatullah Khan, PM Shehbaz said: “He stated that development work is zero, corruption is 100 per cent, and terrorism is at its peak. I completely agree with him.” The premier referred to weaknesses in the police’s performance, stating that arrests in cases of theft and robbery were not made. Mentioning examples of corruption, such as the Kohistan scandal, he said: “You will feel great pain and sorrow over how the province’s resources were looted. God willing, this will be fully controlled, and every single penny of your development and prosperity will be delivered to your doorstep.” Police’s vehicle procurement ban relaxed: Kundi Separately, in a bid to improve the police’s capabilities amid the current law and order situation in the province, Kundi said he has approved the relaxation of the police’s vehicle procurement ban to ensure personnel have the necessary resources. In a post on X, Kundi said that in line with the prevailing security landscape in the province, he approved the relaxation of the ban. “Our [KP police] force stands on the front lines to protect the lives and security of our people,” he wrote. “In the prevailing law and order situation, ensuring that our officers have the vehicles and resources they need is essential to an effective response to security challenges.” Kundi added that the restrictions would be loosened “within the approved scope and against funds already allocated in the Police Procurement Plan”. “This will strengthen operational capacity without placing any additional burden on the provincial exchequer,” he noted. “Supporting our police is not just a responsibility; it is an investment in the safety of our people and the peace of KP.” In July this year, the KP government had imposed a ban on the procurement of vehicles except for ambulances; earth-moving machinery; fire trucks; tractors; trucks; buses; passenger vans; prisoner vans; motorcycles; water tankers; rescue and recovery vehicles and boats; and mobile laboratory vehicles, according to an order issued by the KP finance department. “In case of [an] essential requirement, the chief minister, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, may relax the ban on [a] case-to-case basis,” the order, seen by Dawn , read. Development of merged districts a ‘special priority’ In his address to the apex committee, the KP governor termed establishing peace and stability in KP a “collective priority”, and stressed that it was in the interests of the entire country. Referring to the federal government’s decision to impose emergency and governor’s rule in KP, Kundi said that the peaceful transition showed that the people of the province wanted peace and stability. “I want to pay tribute to my people who showed restraint despite the turmoil,” he said, asserting there had been no untoward incident in the region following the measures. On Oct 14, three days after emergency was imposed, a protest demonstration by PTI workers in Khyber’s Bara tehsil turned violent as protesters clashed with police. Injuries to party workers and cops were reported in the incident. Speaking at the meeting, Kundi also paid tribute to those who sacrificed their lives in the war against terrorism, including personnel of the police, army, Frontier Corps, and Federal Constabulary. “These sacrifices demand a more effective strategy to combat terrorism,” he underscored. The governor reiterated that the foremost priority of his KP Advisory Council was to restore peace and eliminate terrorism. Kundi termed the development of the merged districts a “special priority”. “The people of these regions have paid a heavy price during this fight against terrorism. Now, they deserve better education, health, and economic opportunities,” he declared. “The federal government’s cooperation in establishing peace and stability in the province is very significant,” the PPP leader highlighted, saying he was keen to play his role in this collective endeavour. The governor maintained that the people of KP would not have to choose between peace and development. “This is our collective responsibility to provide people with both.” Kundi declared that the KP Advisory Council would keep playing its role in integrating these merged areas in the circle of national development. “The public’s trust is the only metric of measuring our success in the war on terror,” he asserted, while reaffirming that the whole network of terrorism would be annihilated, and the facilitators and financiers of terrorists would also be targeted. “I seek constant support and supervision by the federal government,” he asked, expressing the hope that the Centre would continue its cooperation. Emergency amid security challenges The Centre had imposed emergency and governor’s rule in KP on Oct 11, citing the PTI-led provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. The decisions were also endorsed by the Parliament last week amid protests by the opposition. Governor Kundi, along with Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, had chaired a meeting of the provincial apex committee a day after governor’s rule was imposed. In the meeting, the governor — who is now in charge of running the province — assured Naqvi he would enforce all policies of the federal government and work together with the security forces for peace and prosperity of the province. Kundi asserted that under the new set-up, tackling terrorism would be the priority. Later that day, Kundi, addressing a press conference, called for greater coordination between the Centre and the province, stressing that policies on counterterrorism will “come from Islamabad [..] not Kabul,” in an apparent jibe at the PTI-led KP government, which has been accused of maintaining a “nexus” with terrorist groups by federal ministers. The Centre’s move to impose governor’s rule and emergency in KP also followed a mobilisation drive and protest march by the PTI and in opposition at the Centre, to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. Intense negotiations between the two sides a week before the imposition of governor’s rule had failed to yield any results, with counterterrorism policy being one of the main reasons behind the breakdown of their talks. The PTI said it was being left out of security decisions concerning KP, which the Centre denied . It also called for reviewing the counterterrorism policy, while the latter criticised the KP government’s efforts to combat terrorism in the province and objected to its stance on dialogue with the Afghan Taliban. Soon after, the Centre also authorised the deployment of Pakistan Army troops and assets in aid of civil power in KP. Federal ministers have also alleged that the PTI-led government in KP had a “nexus” with terrorist groups, stating that the province’s security situation necessitated the imposition of emergency there. Additional input by Irfan Raza

items.title: Programme gouvernemental : l'Alliance de la gauche annonce son vote contre
items.description: Lors de la discussion du programme gouvernemental, jeudi 22 octobre à la Chambre des représentants, Nabila Jalal, députée de l'Alliance de la gauche, a dénoncé le manque d’engagements chiffrés de la nouvelle équipe. Emploi, pouvoir d’achat, services publics, fiscalité et lutte contre la corruption : l’élue a décliné cinq critères à l’aune desquels elle entend juger l’action du gouvernement, avant d’annoncer que son groupe voterait contre le programme. La promesse d’un « changement de cap » ne convainc pas Nabila Jalal. Pour la députée de l'Alliance de la gauche, le programme gouvernemental 2026-2031 ne rompt pas suffisamment avec les pratiques de l’exécutif précédent et reste en deçà des attentes sociales. Jeudi 22 octobre, lors de la discussion du programme à la Chambre des représentants, elle a livré une intervention à charge contre la nouvelle majorité, mettant en cause la crédibilité de ses engagements et l’absence, selon elle, de garanties concrètes pour les mettre en œuvre. D’emblée, l’élue a rappelé la participation de l’actuelle cheffe du gouvernement aux décisions de la précédente équipe, qu’elle accuse d’avoir favorisé « l’alliance flagrante entre l’argent et le pouvoir « , les conflits d’intérêts et les intérêts des lobbies des hydrocarbures. Elle lui reproche également d’avoir contribué à l’appauvrissement de la classe moyenne et des travailleurs, tandis que le capital rentier bénéficiait, selon elle, d’un traitement privilégié. Pour étayer ses critiques, Nabila Jalal a évoqué la saisie de bulletins de vote à Tanger et les suspicions de fraude électorale qui s'en sont suivis, ainsi que la révocation d’une ministre quarante-huit heures après sa nomination, estimant que cet épisode révèle des défaillances dans le choix des responsables et soulève des interrogations sur la capacité de l’exécutif à contrôler des marchés publics de plusieurs milliards de dirhams. Au-delà de ces accusations, la députée a placé le débat sur le terrain de la responsabilité politique. Elle a notamment dénoncé l’absence, dans la déclaration gouvernementale, de mesures qu’elle juge indispensables à une réforme institutionnelle, plaidant notamment pour la reddition des comptes. Cinq critères pour juger le gouvernement Le cœur de son intervention repose sur cinq épreuves censées mesurer la capacité du programme à répondre aux préoccupations des Marocains. La première concerne l’emploi. Nabila Jalal a rappelé que les partis de la majorité avaient promis la création d’un million de postes et une réduction du taux de chômage à 7 % à l’horizon 2031. Elle déplore que la déclaration gouvernementale ne précise ni le nombre d’emplois à créer ni un objectif chiffré de baisse du chômage. Elle regrette également l’absence de référence au salaire minimum, jugeant insuffisante la mise en avant de la formation et de l’expérience professionnelle : « La formation n’est pas un emploi, et l’expérience professionnelle ne constitue pas un contrat de travail », a-t-elle lancé. Le deuxième test porte sur le pouvoir d’achat. L’élue critique le recul, selon elle, de plusieurs promesses électorales. La gratuité automatique et sans conditions de la facture d’électricité aurait ainsi été remplacée par un dispositif d’aide destiné aux ménages considérés comme éligibles. Elle dénonce également le report à une mise en œuvre progressive de l’exonération fiscale des salaires inférieurs à 15.000 dirhams et de la promesse d’une pension de retraite d’au moins 3.000 dirhams. La question du salaire minimum décent, annoncé par un parti allié pour 2027, aurait, elle aussi, été repoussée à la fin du mandat. Sur les hydrocarbures, Nabila Jalal regrette l’absence d’engagement concernant le plafonnement des prix et la remise en service de la raffinerie Samir. Elle estime que les intérêts des détenteurs de monopoles demeurent insuffisamment encadrés. Troisième priorité : la santé et l’éducation. La députée dénonce la dégradation des services publics, le déficit de ressources humaines et le poids du secteur privé, auquel elle attribue 91 % des dépenses de l’assurance-maladie. Elle s’interroge sur les garanties apportées par le programme en matière de gratuité des soins, d’accès à l’enseignement et à l’université, d’augmentation des bourses étudiantes et de financement de la recherche scientifique. Le quatrième critère concerne la justice fiscale. Nabila Jalal met en doute le financement des ambitions économiques affichées par la majorité. Elle relève que son parti mise sur la mobilisation de 300 milliards de dirhams, sur une enveloppe globale de 350 milliards, grâce aux effets additionnels de la croissance. Elle confronte ces projections aux objectifs annoncés par le gouvernement : une croissance de 5 %, un déficit budgétaire inférieur à 3 % et un endettement inférieur à 62 %. La députée reproche surtout à la nouvelle équipe d’avoir relégué au second plan les promesses de taxation des revenus de la rente, des grandes fortunes et des bénéfices issus des monopoles. Elle voit dans les références à l’élargissement de l’assiette fiscale et à la restructuration du portefeuille public le risque d’une nouvelle vague de privatisations. À ses yeux, la protection sociale doit plutôt reposer sur une fiscalité progressive sur la fortune, l’imposition des grands exploitants agricoles et la lutte contre la fraude fiscale. Enfin, le cinquième test porte sur la reddition des comptes. Si le gouvernement affirme que sa responsabilité sera mesurée aux résultats, demande Nabila Jalal, encore faut-il préciser les échéances et les indicateurs permettant de les évaluer. Elle pointe également les contradictions qu’elle perçoit entre la promesse de criminaliser l’enrichissement illicite et la position du ministre de la Justice, issu du parti de la cheffe du gouvernement, qui estime cette mesure contraire à la présomption d’innocence. Des revendications institutionnelles et sociales La critique du programme s’accompagne d’une série de revendications politiques. Sur les libertés publiques, Nabila Jalal a annoncé que son groupe présenterait, pour la troisième fois, une proposition d’amnistie générale en faveur des détenus du Hirak du Rif, des jeunes du mouvement « Génération Z » et des détenus politiques, journalistes, blogueurs, syndicalistes et défenseurs des droits humains. Elle réclame également l’arrêt des poursuites qu’elle qualifie d’abusives et la réparation des préjudices subis. Sur le plan territorial, elle a réaffirmé la revendication de récupération de Sebta et Melilla, des îles et des autres territoires occupés, tout en demandant un programme d’urgence pour les régions frontalières. Elle a plaidé pour que le Parlement et les forces politiques soient associés au débat sur la mise en œuvre du plan d’autonomie. Elle a également défendu une intégration effective de l’amazigh dans les politiques publiques, ainsiqu'une représentation institutionnelle des Marocains du monde. La députée a enfin mis en avant les enjeux de souveraineté hydrique et énergétique, dénonçant l’épuisement des nappes phréatiques par les cultures d’exportation subventionnées et réclamant la remise en service de la raffinerie Samir. Son programme, intitulé « La dignité d’abord », prévoit aussi une réforme de la loi sur la profession d’avocat, une meilleure prise en compte des droits des personnes en situation de handicap, une réforme équitable des retraites et une égalité effective entre les femmes et les hommes dans les postes de décision. Au terme de son intervention, Nabila Jalal a estimé que la déclaration gouvernementale ne répondait à aucune des cinq épreuves qu’elle avait définies. En conséquence, elle a annoncé que son groupe parlementaire voterait contre le programme gouvernemental, tout en promettant d’exercer pleinement ses prérogatives de contrôle et de défendre les propositions de l'Alliance de la gauche. « La dignité des Marocains est une priorité », a-t-elle conclu. The post Programme gouvernemental : l'Alliance de la gauche annonce son vote contre appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .
